arguments.title: Rust
arguments.body:
Rust began as a personal project. In 2006, Graydon Hoare, then an engineer at Mozilla, started tinkering with a small programming language he named after the rust fungus, a nod to the hardy, pervasive organisms that survive by colonizing whatever they touch. Hoare was frustrated by the tradeoff he saw everywhere in systems programming: languages like C and C++ offered speed and control but demanded constant vigilance against memory errors, while garbage-collected languages offered safety at the cost of runtime overhead and unpredictable pauses. He wanted both.

Mozilla took interest and sponsored the project in 2009, and Rust was publicly announced in 2010. The early years were turbulent. The language went through dramatic redesigns, and its compiler, originally written in OCaml, was rewritten in Rust itself in 2011, a milestone known as self-hosting. Features were added, removed, and reworked as the team chased a coherent vision. The most consequential idea to emerge was ownership: a set of compile-time rules governing how memory is allocated, moved, and freed, enforced by a borrow checker that rejects programs which would otherwise cause use-after-free bugs, data races, or double frees. The compiler became famously strict, and the community embraced the resulting error messages as a teaching tool rather than an obstacle.

Rust 1.0 shipped in May 2015, marking the first stable release and a commitment to backward compatibility. Around the same time, the project adopted a formal RFC process and an open governance model, with a core team and numerous working groups. In 2021, the Rust Foundation was established, with Mozilla, AWS, Google, Huawei, Microsoft, and others as founding members, giving the language independent financial and legal footing as Mozilla itself restructured.

Adoption followed steadily. Developers used Rust for command-line tools, web services, embedded systems, and increasingly for the low-level infrastructure of large companies. In 2022, Rust appeared for the first time in the Linux kernel, a landmark for a language long seen as an outsider in systems work. The U.S. government and industry reports began recommending memory-safe languages, further boosting interest.

Today Rust is known for its performance, its expressive type system, its package manager Cargo, and a welcoming community that has repeatedly ranked it among the most loved languages in developer surveys. What started as one engineer's experiment became a serious contender for the future of systems programming.
